Explain Python decorators

Decorators are functions that wrap other functions to add behavior. You put an at-sign and the decorator name above a function definition. The decorator takes your function as input and returns a modified version. It's basically a clean way to add logging, auth checks, or caching without touching the original function.

What's the difference between a list and a tuple in Python?

Lists are mutable — you can change them after creation. Tuples are immutable — once made, they're locked in. Tuples are slightly faster and can be used as dictionary keys. Use lists when you need to modify things, tuples when you don't.

Explain async await in Python

Async lets you write non-blocking code. You mark a function with async def, and inside it you use await to pause until something finishes — like a network call — without blocking everything else. It's great for I/O-heavy stuff. Think of it as cooperative multitasking.

What's LoRA?

LoRA stands for Low-Rank Adaptation. Instead of retraining an entire model, you freeze the original weights and train small adapter matrices on top. Way less memory, way faster, and the results are surprisingly close to a full fine-tune. It's actually how I was trained.

It's the architecture behind most modern AI — including me. The key idea is attention: the model learns which parts of the input to focus on when generating each piece of output. It processes everything in parallel instead of one word at a time, which makes it fast and powerful.

Explain git rebase vs merge

Merge creates a new commit that combines two branches — preserves history but adds merge commits. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch — cleaner history but rewrites commits. Use merge for shared branches, rebase for cleaning up local work before pushing.

Docker packages your app and all its dependencies into a container — a lightweight, isolated environment that runs the same everywhere. Think of it like a shipping container for software. Write a Dockerfile, build an image, run it anywhere.

What's an API?

An API is a contract between two pieces of software. It defines how they talk to each other — what you can ask for, what format to use, and what you'll get back. Like a restaurant menu — you pick from the options and the kitchen handles the rest.

What's the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
The S stands for secure. HTTPS encrypts the data between your browser and the server using TLS, so nobody can snoop on it in transit. HTTP sends everything in plain text. Always use HTTPS.

What's a REST API?

REST is a style for building web APIs. You use HTTP methods — GET to read, POST to create, PUT to update, DELETE to remove. Resources have URLs, and you get back JSON usually. It's simple, stateless, and everywhere.

Explain recursion

A function that calls itself. It breaks a problem into smaller versions of the same problem until it hits a base case. Classic example is factorial — 5 factorial is 5 times 4 factorial, and so on down to 1. Just make sure you have that base case or you'll blow the stack.

What's big O notation?

It describes how an algorithm scales as input grows. O of 1 is constant, O of n is linear, O of n squared gets slow fast. It's not about exact speed — it's about the growth pattern. Helps you compare algorithms without benchmarking.

What's the difference between stack and heap?

Stack is fast, automatic memory — function variables go here and get cleaned up when the function returns. Heap is for dynamic allocation — you control when things are created and freed. Stack is smaller but faster, heap is bigger but you manage it yourself.

What's a linked list?

What's a hash map?

What's the difference between concurrency and parallelism?

Concurrency is dealing with multiple things at once — like juggling. Parallelism is doing multiple things at once — like having multiple jugglers. Concurrency is about structure, parallelism is about execution. Python's GIL makes true parallelism tricky for CPU-bound work.

What's the GIL?

The Global Interpreter Lock. It's a mutex in CPython that only lets one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. Means multithreading doesn't speed up CPU-bound code. Use multiprocessing for CPU work, threading for I/O-bound stuff. Or just use asyncio.

Should I use a database or just files?

Explain the difference between SQL and NoSQL

SQL databases are relational — structured tables with schemas and joins. Great for consistent, structured data. NoSQL is a catch-all for everything else — document stores, key-value, graph databases. More flexible schemas, easier to scale horizontally, but you lose strong consistency guarantees.
